name: surrogate-modeling
title: Surrogate Modeling — can a neural net emulate the v2ecoli baseline?

at_a_glance.role: Roll out the baseline ensemble and build the broad ~11.5k-observable pbg-torch TransitionDataset.
The test: under 8-fold CV the neural net does not beat trivial baselines; one-step R²=1.0 is a persistence artifact; broad panel unlearnable from itself.
What the cheap linear emulator is worth: amortized break-even (~8 evals) plus a 5,000-traj sweep in 0.02 s, and the limits.
Follow-up: does multi-step rollout-loss training close the gap to the linear baseline?

biological_story:
The v2ecoli whole-cell model integrates 55 processes to advance one cell by
one second. A surrogate asks whether a learned function can predict the next
observable state directly and cheaply. The answer is split: the cell's coarse
growth is smooth enough that a linear model emulates it better than a neural
net, while its high-dimensional molecular state is governed by hidden variables
a curated observable view does not carry, so it cannot be predicted from that
view at all. The value is knowing which is which, and having a cheap emulator
for the part that is emulable.
question:
Can a neural-network surrogate, trained on v2ecoli baseline rollouts, emulate
the model's per-step dynamics across a broad observable panel (growth/mass,
exchange fluxes, metabolic fluxes, protein and transcript abundance, chromosome
state), and does it beat trivial baselines enough to justify the complexity?
hypothesis:
We expected a residual-MLP surrogate (via pbg-torch) to emulate the smooth
low-dimensional observables (mass, growth) well, with the high-dimensional
vectors as the hard part. Held to trivial baselines under cross-validation,
that did not survive: the neural net does not beat a linear model on the smooth
target, and the high-dimensional panel is not learnable from the observable
view at all.

executive.what_is_this:
A four-study investigation that builds a neural-network surrogate of the
v2ecoli baseline with pbg-torch
(github.com/vivarium-collective/pbg-torch), then holds it to a skeptical
standard against trivial baselines.

1. sm-00-data-collection: roll out an 8-seed baseline ensemble into a broad ~11.5k-observable pbg-torch TransitionDataset.
2. sm-01-nn-surrogate: does the surrogate beat trivial baselines (persistence, mean-delta, linear) under leave-one-trajectory-out CV?
3. sm-02-utility-and-limits: what the cheap linear emulator is worth — amortized break-even vs. the simulator, and the limits.
4. sm-03-improving-the-surrogate: can multi-step rollout-loss training close the gap?
executive.verdict:
Held to trivial baselines under 8-fold cross-validation, the neural surrogate
does not justify itself: one-step R²≈1.000 is a persistence artifact, and in
multi-step rollout a linear model is the best and most stable emulator of
coarse growth (nRMSE 0.019, 0/8 unstable) while the neural net is no better
and explodes on 2/8 folds. The broad 11.5k-observable panel is not learnable
from the observable view alone (0% of observables beat persistence); it needs
the cell's hidden state. The useful by-product is a cheap linear emulator that
pays for its training data after ~8 evaluations and runs a 5,000-trajectory
sweep in 0.02 s (vs ~24 h on the WCM).

scientific_argument.main_claim:
Under cross-validation against trivial baselines, a neural surrogate does
not beat a linear model at emulating the baseline's smooth observables, and
the high-dimensional cell state is not predictable from a curated observable
view. The useful deliverable is a cheap linear emulator of coarse growth,
not a neural net.
evidence_for: 8-fold CV: linear rollout nRMSE 0.019 (0/8 unstable) is best, beating the neural net (0.032, 2/8 explode) and persistence (1.850).
The cheap emulator pays back its 8 training sims after ~8 evaluations; a 5,000-trajectory sweep runs in 0.02 s vs ~24 h on the WCM.
evidence_against: One-step R²≈1.000 looks like strong emulation but is a persistence artifact (persistence also scores 1.000), not learned dynamics.
caveats: Trained on 8 single-generation local trajectories; the cheap emulator covers coarse, smooth observables only.
The negative result is conditioned on this observable panel and modest data; sm-03 tests whether better training narrows the gap.

studies.name: sm-00-data-collection
studies.title: Surrogate data collection — broad observable transition-dataset from baseline rollouts
studies.question:
Can the deeply-nested baseline state (pint Quantities, per-agent keys,
dict-valued exchange fluxes, high-dimensional count/flux vectors) be extracted
into a stable, flat (state_t, state_t+1) transition dataset covering every
observable category?
studies.claim:
An 8-seed ensemble of baseline rollouts can be flattened into a single
pbg-torch TransitionDataset spanning a broad observable panel (growth/mass,
exchange fluxes, metabolic fluxes, protein and transcript abundance,
chromosome state) — ~11.5k observables per step — suitable for training a
neural-network surrogate.

studies.name: sm-01-nn-surrogate
studies.title: NN surrogate — does it beat trivial baselines?
studies.question:
Does the neural-network surrogate beat trivial baselines (persistence,
mean-delta, linear) on the baseline's per-step dynamics — and are the
high-dimensional observables learnable from the observable view at all?
studies.claim:
Tested honestly against trivial baselines under cross-validation, the neural
surrogate does NOT beat them: one-step R²≈1.0 is a persistence artifact (the
signal is smooth), and in multi-step rollout a LINEAR model is the best and
most stable emulator of coarse growth/mass while the neural net matches it at
best and destabilizes on 2/8 folds. The broad ~11.5k-observable panel is not
learnable from the observable view alone (0% of observables beat persistence).
A neural surrogate is not justified for these targets on this evidence.

studies.name: sm-02-utility-and-limits
studies.title: Utility & limits — what a cheap emulator buys, and where emulation ends
studies.question:
Given that the linear emulator (not the neural net) is the model that works
for coarse growth, is it actually worth building — i.e. does it amortize
against the cost of generating its training data — and what are its limits?
studies.claim:
The honest by-product of sm-01 — a cheap LINEAR emulator of coarse growth —
is genuinely useful: it pays back its 8 training simulations after ~8
evaluations and sweeps 5,000 trajectories in 0.02 s (vs ~24 h on the WCM,
~3.8e6× per trajectory). Its limits are explicit: it emulates a smooth,
low-dimensional observable view, not the cell's high-dimensional hidden state.

studies.name: sm-03-improving-the-surrogate
studies.title: Improving the surrogate — does rollout-loss training close the gap?
studies.question:
sm-01 diagnosed the neural net's weakness as autoregressive instability from
one-step training. Does the principled fix — multi-step rollout-loss training —
close the gap to the linear baseline?
studies.claim:
Multi-step rollout-loss training (the net trains on its own unrolled
predictions) genuinely improves the neural surrogate — it eliminates the
autoregressive instability (0/8 unstable folds vs 1/8 for one-step training)
and lowers rollout error (median nRMSE 0.053 vs 0.069). It still does not beat
the linear baseline (0.019) for this smooth target, but it is the right
technique to carry to harder, genuinely nonlinear targets.
